newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish "dream" budget unlikely to become reality.
newsitem.headline: Turkish "dream" budget unlikely to become reality.

text.p: Turkey is likely to face a larger budget deficit next year despite Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's zero-deficit target because of unrealistic revenue forecasts, analysts said on Sunday.
Erbakan described his $46.3 billion 1997 draft budget as a revolution in the 73-year history of the Turkish republic. Analysts and the opposition think "he is just dreaming."

"If a prime minister says he will make a balanced budget next year in a country whose budget is expected to give a deficit of 10 percent of the gross national product this year, no one believes him," said Osman Ulagay, a columnist at the daily Milliyet.
Economists predict the 1997 bugdet submitted to parliament last week would give a deficit of around $18.5 billion, up from $16 billion expected this year.
The 1997 budget draft was built on several weak assumptions, analysts said.
It envisages raising $3.5 billion by selling a minority stake in the Turk Telekom communications giant.

However, privatisation analysts say the sale may take 12 to 18 months and note the government has not tried to further the sell-off since Telekom's privatisation was hindered by a court ruling in February.

The government hopes to generate an additional $5.2 billion by selling other state assets, including public properties -- well above the $3 billion Turkey has raised since it started privatisation in 1986.
Economists say it is very risky to pin hopes of a zero deficit on privatisation targets that were missed by substantial margins in the past decade.
Turkey set a $5 billion target in 1995 but sold only $515 million of state assets. Of this year's target of around $2 billion, only $292 million has been raised so far.

"We think that the (1997) budget will give a deficit. A balanced budget is seen very difficult (to attain)," said Suhan Seckin, general manager of Toros Securities. "This can happen only through privatisation."

Turkey's failing credibility in international markets, lack of domestic capital, legal barriers and populist concerns of the ruling parties are seen as major obstacles to privatisation on the scale Erbakan needs.
Ulagay said the target of a sharp rise in the government's non-tax revenues was an "illusion."
The Islamist-led coalition government calls for no tax reform but foresees a 100 percent increase in 1997 tax revenues, up from the inflation target of 65 percent.

On the expenditure side, the government forecast a sharp fall of about $5 billion in foreign and domestic debt interest payments because hoped-for privatisation revenues would cut the borrowing requirement and lower short-term interest rates.
But bankers warn that any government attempt to lower interest rates artificially could spark a run on the lira.
